topic: The Secret Identity of the Potato: Is it a Root or a Stem?

sections.title: The Culinary Mystery: Root or Stem?
lecture_lines: It grows underground, so is a potato a root?
Meet Chef Spud, who is confused about his ingredients.
Let's investigate the biological identity of this popular veggie.
animations: Show a cross-section of soil (#8B4513) with a potato (#D2B48C) and a carrot (#FFA500) positioned underground.
A simple white chef hat (#FFFFFF) appears above the potato and tilts left and right to represent Chef Spud's confusion.
A magnifying glass (#B0C4DE) moves over the potato as the soil fades out, leaving only the potato and carrot on the #000000 background.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Anatomy of a Stem
lecture_lines: To solve this, we must identify stem markers.
Nodes are the specific points where leaves grow.
Internodes are the spaces found between these nodes.
Axillary buds wait at nodes to sprout new growth.
Roots lack these organized segments and buds entirely.
animations: A simple vertical green line (#32CD32) representing a plant stem appears in the center of the screen.
Horizontal blue lines (#00BFFF) appear at regular intervals on the stem, each labeled 'Nodes' in white text.
The segments of the stem between the blue lines glow yellow (#FFFFE0) and are labeled 'Internodes'.
Small green circles (#00FF00) appear at each node intersection, labeled 'Axillary Buds'.
A brownish root shape (#CD853F) appears to the right; it is smooth and lacks any node markings or buds.

sections.title: Defining the Tuber: A Specialized Storage Tank
lecture_lines: A tuber is a modified plant part storing energy.
Starch travels down the phloem to underground storage.
Tubers can originate from either stems or roots.
animations: A plant above ground is shown connected to a beige storage bulb (#DEB887) beneath the soil surface.
White particles (#FFFFFF) flow down a blue tube (#4169E1) from the leaves into the bulb, causing it to expand slightly.
Text labels 'Stem Tuber' and 'Root Tuber' appear with arrows pointing from the main plant structure to different underground parts.

sections.title: The 'Eyes' Have It: Examining the Potato
lecture_lines: Look closely at the "eyes" on a potato's surface.
These eyes are actually nodes with axillary buds.
In the dark, these buds sprout into new stems.
True roots, like carrots, cannot sprout this way.
This structural evidence proves the potato is a stem.
animations: A large tan potato (#D2B48C) appears with dark brown spots (#4B3621) labeled 'Eyes'.
Blue circles (#00BFFF) highlight the 'eyes,' and the label updates to 'Nodes with Buds'.
Bright green sprouts (#32CD32) grow outwards from several of the highlighted 'eyes' to simulate stem growth.
An orange carrot (#FFA500) appears next to the potato; it remains static and does not grow any sprouts.
The potato with sprouts is positioned next to the stem diagram from Section 2 to show matching node patterns, with a 'Stem' label appearing.

sections.title: The Great Comparison: Potato vs. Sweet Potato
lecture_lines: Compare the potato to its cousin, the sweet potato.
The potato is a stem tuber with visible nodes.
The sweet potato is a root tuber without nodes.
X-rays reveal the potato's internal stem-like pith.
Sweet potatoes have a central core and lateral roots.
animations: A potato (#D2B48C) and a sweet potato (#A0522D) are shown side-by-side for comparison.
Blue rings (#00BFFF) highlight the 'eyes' (nodes) on the potato.
The sweet potato is highlighted, showing its smooth surface with no nodes or eyes.
The potato becomes semi-transparent, revealing a vertical central pith (#F0E68C) characteristic of stems.
The sweet potato reveals a thick central core (#DEB887) and thin stringy lateral roots (#CD853F) branching out from the sides.

sections.title: Summary: The Verdict
lecture_lines: The verdict is in: the potato is a stem.
Classification depends on structure, not just location.
Case closed on this underground biological mystery!
animations: A large green checkmark (#00FF00) and the word 'STEM' in bold white text appear over the potato image.
A diagram showing the potato plant highlights the underground stem (#32CD32) that connects the tuber to the main stalk.
A red 'CASE CLOSED' stamp (#FF0000) appears in the center of the screen over the finalized diagram.
